claim: Approximately 50% of splicing changes (corrected p-value ≤ 0.25 and |ΔPSI| ≥ 10) were classified as alternative first exon (AFE) events following LPS activation in both human and murine macrophages.
source: We found that ~50% of splicing changes (corrected p-value ≤ 0.25 and |ΔPSI| ≥ 10) were classified as AFE events following LPS activation in both human and murine macrophages (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, representing experimental measurements.

claim: AFE events consistently comprised a large proportion of the top splicing changes in both mouse and human data sets.
source: A ranking analysis of the significant events, from both mouse and human data sets, revealed that AFE events consistently comprised a large proportion of the top splicing changes (Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by ranking analysis of RNA-seq data presented in supplementary figures.

claim: Analysis of previously published primary human macrophages stimulated with either Listeria or Salmonella revealed AFE events to be amongst the most significant prevalent alternative splicing events.
source: Additionally, analysis of previously published primary human macrophages stimulated with either Listeria or Salmonella, using our bioinformatic pipeline and with more stringent thresholds than the previous study, also revealed AFE events to be amongst the most significant prevalent alternative splicing events (corrected p-value ≤ 0.05 or 0.25 and |ΔPSI| ≥ 10) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4; Supplementary files 4-5–; Pai et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by reanalysis of published data (Pai et al., 2016) using the authors' bioinformatic pipeline, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Eleven conserved AFE splicing events were identified between human and mouse macrophages.
source: We next identified 11 conserved AFE splicing events between human and mouse (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A,B), the largest number of conserved event types amongst all alternative splicing event types (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analysis of RNA-seq data from human and mouse macrophages, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: AFE changes in Ncoa7 upon stimulation were validated in human and mouse primary macrophages using RT-PCR.
source: We validated the AFE changes upon stimulation on the already characterized Ncoa7 (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A–C; Singer et al., 2008; Yu et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6A-C and references to prior characterization studies.

claim: AFE changes in Rcan1 upon stimulation were validated in human and mouse primary macrophages using RT-PCR.
source: We validated the AFE changes upon stimulation on the already characterized...Rcan1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 6D–F; Pang et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6D-F and a reference to prior characterization.

claim: A previously uncharacterized inflammatory-specific isoform of Ampd3 was validated in human and mouse primary macrophages using RT-PCR.
source: as well as a previously uncharacterized inflammatory-specific isoform of Ampd3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 6G–I), in human and mouse primary macrophages using RT-PCR.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6G-I.

claim: Native RNA-sequencing of murine macrophages with and without LPS treatment was performed to build a de novo murine macrophage specific transcriptome with an average read depth of 1 million.
source: we performed native RNA-sequencing of murine macrophages with and without LPS treatment to build a de novo murine macrophage specific transcriptome with an average read depth of 1 million.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental approach and sequencing depth achieved.

claim: The incorporation of long-read sequencing to generate a novel transcriptome led to the identification of 95 novel and statistically significant AFE events that occur following inflammation.
source: Overall, the incorporation of long-read sequencing to generate a novel transcriptome led to the identification of 95 novel and statistically significant AFE events that occur following inflammation (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of long-read sequencing data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Novel TSSs identified with FLAIR showed a 45% overlap with CAGE-seq peaks classified as true.
source: Novel TSSs identified with FLAIR showed a 45% overlap with CAGE-seq peaks classified as true, providing us with confidence in the novel AFE events identified (Figure 1—figure supplement 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of FLAIR-identified TSSs with CAGE-seq data, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8C.

claim: Approximately 50% of genes with AFE usage were not differentially expressed following inflammation.
source: Interestingly, when identifying gene expression changes, we found that ~50% of genes with AFE usage were not differentially expressed following inflammation (Figure 1E,F; Supplementary files 6–7)
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 1E,F and supplementary files.

claim: Denr, Arhgef7, and Aim2 are among the most statistically significant novel AFE first exon events.
source: Among the most statistically significant novel AFE first exon events were Denr, Arhgef7, and Aim2, which we validated using RT-qPCR (Figure 1G–I, Figure 1—figure supplement 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and RT-qPCR validation shown in Figure 1G-I and Figure 1—figure supplement 9.

claim: ChIP-seq for PU.1 in primary BMDMs supported the presence of an additional promoter upstream of the canonical isoform for Aim2.
source: Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP)-seq for the myeloid pioneering TF PU.1 in primary BMDMs (Figure 2A,B, top track, in black) (Lam et al., 2013) supported the presence of an additional promoter upstream of the canonical isoform for Aim2 (NM_001013779.2).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data from Lam et al., 2013 shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Predominant isoforms assembled from native RNA-sequencing with FLAIR identified the canonical isoform and five unannotated isoforms of Aim2 that use the inflammatory-activated promoter.
source: Predominant isoforms (≥10% of total gene expression in a sample) assembled from native RNA-sequencing with FLAIR identified the canonical isoform and five unannotated isoforms that use the inflammatory-activated promoter, revealing a new longer 5′UTR (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by FLAIR analysis of native RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: At steady state, approximately 20% of Aim2 reads map to the transcript with the canonical promoter and 65% map to transcripts with the upstream promoter.
source: At steady state, approximately 20% of reads map to Aim2's transcript with the canonical promoter and 65% of reads map to transcripts with the upstream promoter
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of native RNA-sequencing reads.

claim: Following inflammatory activation, 14% of Aim2 reads map to transcripts with the canonical promoter and 81% map to transcripts with the upstream promoter.
source: while following inflammatory activation, 14% of the reads map to transcripts with the canonical promoter and 81% of reads map to transcripts with the upstream promoter (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of native RNA-sequencing reads shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The expression profile of the annotated first exon of Aim2 is not induced by LPS stimulation.
source: The expression profile of the annotated first exon is not induced by LPS stimulation (Figure 2F)
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The unannotated first exon and the CDS of Aim2 are equally induced by LPS stimulation.
source: while the unannotated first exon and the CDS of Aim2 are equally induced by LPS stimulation (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2G,H.

claim: It is the novel isoform of Aim2 that is inflammatory-regulated and not the canonical isoform defined in GENCODE annotation.
source: Therefore, these data show that it is the novel isoform of Aim2 that is inflammatory-regulated and not the canonical isoform defined in GENCODE annotation, nor isoforms from the RefSeq annotation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the RT-qPCR and sequencing data showing differential regulation of the novel versus canonical isoforms.

claim: Analysis of ATAC-Seq revealed differential peaks at the promoter regions for 25% of genes with significant AFE events.
source: Analysis of ATAC-Seq (Tong et al., 2016) revealed differential peaks at the promoter regions for 25% of genes with significant AFE events, suggesting that chromatin remodeling is one mechanism driving the expression of the AFE events (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq analysis from Tong et al., 2016 shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The accessibility of both the annotated and unannotated Aim2 promoters remains open despite the cell's inflammatory status.
source: In addition, the accessibility of both the annotated and unannotated promoters remains open despite the cell's inflammatory status (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The expression of the new Aim2 isoform is not due to chromatin remodeling of either promoter region.
source: Therefore, the expression of the new isoform is not due to chromatin remodeling of either promoter region (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is inferred from ATAC-seq data showing constitutive accessibility shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: p65 and IRF3 specifically account for another 25% of the AFE events, including the novel Aim2 isoform.
source: We found that p65 and IRF3 specifically account for another 25% of the AFE events, including the novel Aim2 isoform, which we confirmed using multiple ChIP-seq data sets (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: There are 304 potential transcription factors that bind AFE promoters.
source: Further bioinformatic analysis of promoters associated with all AFEs, using HOMER TF motif enrichment, shows that there are 304 potential TFs that bind these promoters.
evidence: The claim is supported by HOMER TF motif enrichment analysis.

claim: The majority of transcription factors binding AFE promoters are associated with metabolism and the immune system.
source: By gene ontology analysis, we see that the majority of the TFs are associated with metabolism, as well as the immune system (Figure 3B; Supplementary file 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 3B and Supplementary file 10.

claim: There are 106 individual TF motifs within the annotated promoter of Aim2 and 121 motifs within the unannotated promoter.
source: When specifically assessing the two promoter regions driving the annotated and unannotated isoforms of Aim2, we identified 106 individual TF motifs within the annotated promoter and 121 motifs within the unannotated promoter (Supplementary file 11).
evidence: The claim is supported by TF motif analysis documented in Supplementary file 11.

claim: There are 44 TF motifs unique to the unannotated Aim2 promoter.
source: Of these predicted motifs, there were 44 motifs unique to the unannotated promoter (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative motif analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The unannotated Aim2 promoter is driven by inflammatory-specific TFs including NF-κB and IRFs.
source: Gene ontology (Huang et al., 2007) analysis of TFs specific to the annotated and unannotated promoter regions of Aim2 confirms that the unannotated promoter is driven by inflammatory-specific TFs including NF-κB and IRFs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2L).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2L and references the Huang et al., 2007 method.

claim: Use of ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq for specific TFs has enabled determination of the regulatory pathways driving 50% of the AFEs.
source: Use of ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq for specific TFs has enabled us to determine the regulatory pathways driving 50% of the AFEs in our data.
evidence: The claim summarizes the results from ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq analyses.

claim: The novel inflammatory isoform of Aim2 acquired a longer 5′UTR (767 bp) compared to the canonical isoform (489 bp).
source: The novel inflammatory isoform identified here for Aim2 acquired a longer 5′UTR compared to the canonical isoform; however, globally there are no differences in AFE size between conditions (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 4A and supplementary figures.

claim: Globally there are no differences in AFE size between control and LPS conditions.
source: The novel inflammatory isoform identified here for Aim2 acquired a longer 5′UTR compared to the canonical isoform; however, globally there are no differences in AFE size between conditions (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by global analysis of AFE sizes shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The unannotated Aim2 5′UTR showed significantly lower mean GFP fluorescence units compared to the annotated 5′UTR in 293T cells.
source: The unannotated 5′UTR showed significantly lower mean GFP fluorescence units, suggestive of lower translational efficiency, as assessed by flow cytometry 72 hr post-transient transfection in 293T cells (Figure 4C,D)
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data from GFP reporter assays shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: A single IRE was identified within the unannotated Aim2 5′UTR using RegRNA2.0.
source: We identified a single IRE within the unannotated 5′UTR, while Musashi binding element (MBE) motifs were identified in both 5′UTRs (Figure 4F; Supplementary file 14).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational motif prediction using RegRNA2.0 shown in Figure 4F and Supplementary file 14.

claim: There are more predicted motifs in inflammatory-regulated first exons (inclusion exons) compared to basal exons (excluded exons).
source: Globally, we find that there are more predicted motifs in inflammatory-regulated first exons (inclusion exons) in comparison to basal exons (excluded exons), but the IRE motif is found only in Aim2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by global motif analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The IRE motif is found only in Aim2 among the AFE events analyzed.
source: Globally, we find that there are more predicted motifs in inflammatory-regulated first exons (inclusion exons) in comparison to basal exons (excluded exons), but the IRE motif is found only in Aim2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by global motif analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Removal of the IRE element from the unannotated Aim2 5′UTR led to an increase in GFP expression by approximately 20% compared to the annotated 5′UTR.
source: To experimentally test if the IRE motif within the unannotated 5′UTR acts as a translational repressor, we removed the element using site-directed mutagenesis, which led to an increase in GFP expression by ~20% compared to the annotated 5′UTR (Figure 4H,I).
evidence: The claim is supported by GFP reporter assay data following site-directed mutagenesis shown in Figure 4H,I.

claim: Upon FAC administration, the relative GFP expression of the unannotated Aim2 5′UTR plasmid increased by approximately 50%.
source: Upon FAC administration, the relative GFP expression of the unannotated 5′UTR plasmid increased by ~50%, while mCherry control was unchanged, suggesting that the translational efficiency of the unannotated 5′UTR can be rescued with iron supplementation (Figure 4J,K).
evidence: The claim is supported by GFP reporter assay data with iron supplementation shown in Figure 4J,K.

claim: Neat1 is not detected in polysomes and is not translated, independent of LPS treatment.
source: As a negative control, we examined Neat1 (Nakagawa et al., 2014), a long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) that is not detected in polysomes, nor translated, and this is not dependent on LPS (Figure 4N).
evidence: The claim is supported by polysome profiling data shown in Figure 4N and references Nakagawa et al., 2014.

claim: Gapdh is enriched in the high polysome fraction with or without LPS treatment.
source: The relative distribution of our positive control gene, Gapdh, which encodes a highly expressed housekeeping protein, is enriched in the high polysome fraction, with or without LPS, as expected (Figure 4O).
evidence: The claim is supported by polysome profiling data shown in Figure 4O.

claim: The annotated Aim2 isoform is enriched in the high polysome fraction with and without LPS treatment.
source: Using isoform-specific primer sets (Figure 2E) for the annotated and unannotated Aim2 isoforms, we find that the annotated isoform is enriched in the high polysome fraction with and without LPS treatment (Figure 4P)
evidence: The claim is supported by polysome profiling followed by RT-qPCR shown in Figure 4P.

claim: The novel Aim2 isoform is enriched in the low polysome fraction with and without inflammatory stimulation.
source: while the novel isoform is enriched in the low polysome fraction with and without inflammatory stimulation (Figure 4Q).
evidence: The claim is supported by polysome profiling followed by RT-qPCR shown in Figure 4Q.

claim: IRP1 and IRP2 are not transcriptionally regulated by inflammation in BMDMs.
source: Additionally, from our RNA-seq data we find that IRP1 and IRP2 are not transcriptionally regulated by inflammation, but based on Weiss et al. inflammation can affect the binding affinity of IRPs in macrophages (Weiss et al., 1997; Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A-D and references Weiss et al., 1997.

claim: Aim2 protein is expressed basally and significantly decreases upon LPS treatment at the 48 hr time point in primary BMDMs.
source: Aim2 is expressed basally and significantly decreases upon LPS treatment at the 48 hr time point, most likely as a control mechanism to return the pathway to homeostasis and limit the inflammatory stimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data from time-course LPS stimulation experiments.

claim: When FAC is added to cells, Aim2 expression does not decrease at the 48 hr time point.
source: When FAC is added to cells, Aim2 expression does not decrease at the 48 hr time point suggesting that it is indeed the IRE that is driving this decrease in Aim2 observed in the wild type cells (Figure 4R-SFigure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data with iron supplementation shown in Figure 4R-S.

claim: The annotated Aim2 isoform shows no induction by LPS in IRE KO immortalized BMDMs.
source: The annotated Aim2 isoform shows no induction by LPS (Figure 4—figure supplement 4C)
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from IRE KO cells shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4C.

claim: The unannotated Aim2 isoform and the CDS sequence are induced by twofold in IRE KO immortalized BMDMs.
source: while the unannotated Aim2 isoform and the CDS sequence are induced by twofold (Figure 4—figure supplement 4D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from IRE KO cells shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4D,E.

claim: There is no significant difference in transcriptional expression at the Aim2 locus between WT and IRE KO cell lines.
source: There is no significant difference in transcriptional expression at the Aim2 locus between the WT and IRE KO cell lines (Figure 4—figure supplement 4D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR comparison between WT and IRE KO cells shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4D,E.

claim: At the 48 hr time point, there is a significant decrease in expression of Aim2 protein in WT cells but not in IRE KO cells.
source: At the 48 hr time point, there is a significant decrease in expression of Aim2 protein in WT cells, but not in the IRE KO cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 4H), further indicating that endogenous Aim2 is regulated through the IRE motif located in the AFE.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data comparing WT and IRE KO cells shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4H.

claim: Macrophages are critical cells in the innate immune system that combat infection by initiating acute inflammatory responses.
source: Macrophages are critical cells in the innate immune system that combat infection by initiating acute inflammatory responses.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about macrophage function.

claim: Acute inflammation begins with the detection of pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) by pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), which include toll-like receptors (TLRs).
source: Acute inflammation is tightly coordinated and begins with the detection of pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) by pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), which include toll-ike receptors (TLRs) (Medzhitov and Janeway, 1998; Pai et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Medzhitov and Janeway, 1998 and Pai et al., 2016.

claim: Pattern recognition receptor activation is followed by the activation of sequestered transcription factors such as NF-κB and IRFs.
source: These initial steps are followed by the activation of sequestered transcription factors (TFs), such as nuclear factor of kappa-B (NF-κB) and interferon regulatory factors (IRFs), which orchestrate pro-inflammatory and antiviral response signals involved in pathogen clearance (Pai et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pai et al., 2016 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Once pathogens are cleared, macrophages express genes involved in the resolution of inflammation to return the host to homeostasis.
source: Once pathogens are cleared, macrophages express genes involved in the resolution of inflammation to return the host to homeostasis (Hamidzadeh et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hamidzadeh et al., 2017.

claim: Dysregulation of pro-inflammatory pathways can lead to unresolved inflammation and chronic inflammatory diseases.
source: Dysregulation of these pro-inflammatory pathways can have devastating consequences, leading to unresolved inflammation and chronic inflammatory diseases (Zhou et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2016.

claim: Alternative splicing is a regulated process enabling a single gene to produce many isoforms, thus increasing the complexity of gene function and the proteome.
source: Alternative splicing is a regulated process enabling a single gene to produce many isoforms, thus increasing the complexity of gene function and the proteome (Boudreault et al., 2016; Ivanov and Anderson, 2013; Pai et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: Much of alternative splicing occurs in a cell-type-specific and signal-induced manner.
source: Much of this occurs in a cell-type-specific and signal-induced manner (Ergun et al., 2013; Wells et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ergun et al., 2013 and Wells et al., 2006.

claim: Mouse and human macrophages exposed to inflammatory stimuli undergo alternative splicing.
source: Previous studies have shown that mouse and human macrophages exposed to inflammatory stimuli undergo alternative splicing (Beyer et al., 2012; Bhatt et al., 2012; de Bruin et al., 2016; Haque et al., 2018; Janssen et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2018; O'Connor et al., 2015; Pai et al., 2016; Pandya-Jones et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: A soluble form of TLR4 is expressed upon LPS stimulation and leads to inhibition of TNFα and NF-κB, serving as a negative feedback mechanism.
source: Alternative splicing within the immune system can affect the type and magnitude of the inflammatory response, such as the production of a soluble form of TLR4 that is expressed upon lipopolysaccharide (LPS), which leads to inhibition of TNFα and NF-κB serving as a negative feedback mechanism (Lynch, 2004; Schaub and Glasmacher, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lynch, 2004 and Schaub and Glasmacher, 2017.

claim: TBK1s and MyD88s are alternative RNA splice forms that function to limit the extent of the pro-inflammatory response.
source: Additionally, this mechanism has been characterized within signaling molecules (Blumhagen et al., 2017; Shakola et al., 2015), including TBK1 (Deng et al., 2008) and MyD88 (De Arras and Alper, 2013), that produce the alternative RNA splice forms, TBK1s and MyD88s, respectively, which function to limit the extent of the pro-inflammatory response.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Alternative splicing can result in the production of inflammatory signaling molecules such as TRIF and proteins in the NFκB family with altered activity or stability.
source: Alternative splicing can also result in the production of inflammatory signaling molecules, such as TRIF (Han et al., 2010) and the proteins in the NFκB family (Wells et al., 2006) with altered activity or stability.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Han et al., 2010 and Wells et al., 2006.

claim: Elongating or shortening the first or last exon can impact post-transcriptional gene regulation.
source: Beyond changing the ORF of an mRNA molecule, elongating or shortening the first or last exon can impact post-transcriptional gene regulation and are important to consider when elucidating the regulatory mechanisms of immune genes (Carpenter et al., 2014; Ghiasvand et al., 2014; Leppek et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Carpenter et al., 2014, Ghiasvand et al., 2014, and Leppek et al., 2018.

claim: Long-read RNA-sequencing has not been utilized to generate a de novo transcriptome for primary murine macrophages prior to this study.
source: While inflammation-induced alternative splicing in both human and mouse macrophages has been investigated on a genome-wide scale (Beyer et al., 2012; Bhatt et al., 2012; de Bruin et al., 2016; Haque et al., 2018; Janssen et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2018; O'Connor et al., 2015; Pai et al., 2016; Pandya-Jones et al., 2013), to our knowledge, long-read RNA-sequencing has not been utilized to generate a de novo transcriptome for primary murine macrophages.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature and multiple citations.

claim: Most transcriptome annotations are incomplete.
source: Such an approach is necessary to fully appreciate the extent of alternative transcript isoform usage as we know most transcriptome annotations are incomplete (Workman et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Workman et al., 2019.

claim: Isoforms generated are cell-type and treatment specific.
source: and isoforms generated are cell-type and treatment specific (Sapkota et al., 2019; Weirather et al., 2017; Workman et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: AFE events can have multilevel effects on protein diversity, regulating genes through alterations of the 5′UTR region and directing the locality of proteins through alternative N-termini.
source: AFE events can have multilevel effects on protein diversity, regulating genes through alterations of the 5′UTR region, and directing the locality of proteins through alternative N-termini (Landry et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Landry et al., 2003.

claim: The unannotated AFE isoform of Aim2 is the predominant isoform produced during inflammation.
source: We show that this unannotated AFE isoform of Aim2 is the predominant isoform produced during inflammation
evidence: The claim is supported by native RNA-sequencing and RT-qPCR data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The unannotated AFE isoform of Aim2 contains an iron-responsive element in its 5′UTR enabling mRNA translation to be controlled by iron levels.
source: and contains an iron-responsive element (IRE) in its 5′UTR, enabling mRNA translation to be controlled by iron levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by motif prediction, GFP reporter assays, polysome profiling, and western blot experiments.

claim: Aim2 is an interferon-stimulated gene localized to the cytosol.
source: Aim2 is an interferon-stimulated gene (ISG), localized to the cytosol.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Aim2.

claim: Aim2 is a dsDNA sensor that upon recognition induces the formation of an inflammasome complex releasing IL1β and IL18 from the cell.
source: Aim2 is a dsDNA sensor that upon recognition induces the formation of an inflammasome complex releasing IL1β and IL18 from the cell as a defense mechanism to control infection (Wang and Yin, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wang and Yin, 2017 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Alternative transcript isoform usage plays a crucial role in shaping the transient nature of the inflammatory response.
source: This work reveals that alternative transcript isoform usage plays a crucial role in shaping the transient nature of the inflammatory response.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Isoform expression is an additional layer of regulation within the immune response and a possible contributing factor to the development of auto-immune and inflammatory diseases.
source: Isoform expression is an additional layer of regulation within the immune response and therefore a possible contributing factor to the development of auto-immune and inflammatory diseases.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the findings and their potential implications.

claim: Understanding the exact isoforms of genes expressed during an inflammatory response will enable better design of targets for therapeutic intervention of inflammatory diseases.
source: Understanding the exact isoforms of genes that are expressed during an inflammatory response will enable us to design better targets for therapeutic intervention of these diseases.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential applications of the research.

claim: ROS can contribute to activation of Aim2 inflammasome in mouse macrophages.
source: Crane et al., 2014 demonstrate that ROS can contribute to activation of Aim2 inflammasome in mouse macrophages.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Crane et al., 2014.

claim: IRP2 degradation can be driven not only through iron but also through ROS and RNS.
source: Interestingly, IRP2 degradation can be driven not only through iron, but also through ROS and RNS (Hanson and Leibold, 1999)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hanson and Leibold, 1999.

claim: AIM2 is regulated by oxidative stress and overactivation of AIM2 inflammasome can contribute to pancreatic tumorigenesis within the environment of mitochondrial iron overload.
source: Finally, Cheng et al. have shown that AIM2 is regulated by oxidative stress and show that overactivation of AIM2 inflammasome can contribute to pancreatic tumorigenesis, all within the environment of mitochondrial iron overload (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2018.

claim: AIM2 expression levels have been correlated with severity of inflammation in SLE patients.
source: AIM2 expression levels have been correlated with severity of inflammation in SLE patients (Zhang et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: Iron is dysregulated in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
source: and it is well known that iron is dysregulated in this disease (Vanarsa et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Vanarsa et al., 2012.

claim: It is possible that AIM2 levels remain high in SLE patients due to dysregulated iron, preventing homeostasis in macrophages.
source: It is possible that AIM2 levels remain high in SLE patients due to dysregulated iron; therefore, homeostasis in macrophages cannot be maintained.
evidence: This is a speculative statement connecting the findings to SLE pathology.

claim: A better understanding of the molecular mechanisms that control inflammatory-regulated genes could provide new targets for therapeutic intervention of autoimmune and inflammatory diseases.
source: A better understanding of the molecular mechanisms that control inflammatory-regulated genes, including Aim2, could provide new targets for therapeutic intervention of autoimmune and inflammatory diseases.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications of the research.
